summary: Specifies a standard form for sending internationalized text across networks, much as ASCII was used in the early ARPANET. It uses UTF-8 with normalization and specific line-ending sequences. It replaces RFC 698. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC says how text should be written when it travels over the Internet. It uses the Unicode character set in UTF-8, so any language can be sent, and it adds two rules that keep text comparable: lines end with a carriage return and line feed, and the text is put into a single normal form before it is sent.

subtitle: A standard way to send text in any language over the Internet: UTF-8, normalized, with CRLF line endings.

tldr.problem: Internet protocols grew up around a single character set, ASCII, so text in other scripts had no agreed form on the wire, and the same text could be written in more than one way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Net-Unicode: characters encoded in UTF-8, line endings written as a carriage return followed by a line feed, text normalized in Unicode form NFC before transmission, no byte order mark, and no characters that the sender's Unicode version has not assigned.
tldr.outcome: Net-Unicode replaces RFC 698 as the agreed international text format for the Internet, and it updates the character set policy of RFC 854.

facts.label: Line ending
facts.value: Carriage return and line feed (U+000D, U+000A)

facts.label: Byte order mark
facts.value: Must not appear at the start of the string

today: RFC 5198 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 698 and updated the character set policy of RFC 854.

sections.title: Why a Standard Text Format Is Needed
sections.content:
Internet protocols have largely assumed that text means ASCII, the seven-bit character set fixed at the start of the ARPANET, and usually the Network Virtual Terminal form of it. Protocols that went beyond ASCII had to add arrangements to say which character set, and often which language, they were using.

That no longer works. Unicode has become the single international character coding, so there is no longer one standard per script. Using Unicode, however, is more ambiguous than using ASCII was, because Unicode can be turned into bytes in several standard ways. UTF-8 is a variable-length encoding that applies to every code point. UTF-16 encodes the code points below 65536 directly as 16-bit integers and uses surrogates for the rest. UTF-32, also known as UCS-4, encodes every code point as a 32-bit integer. Unicode numbers its characters, with each one called a code point, in the range 0 to 0x10ffff.

Line endings are a further source of confusion, because each of these encodings can be combined with different conventions for ending a line, which matters when a protocol counts characters by position. The RFC therefore proposes Net-Unicode as a standard text form for the Internet: the internationalized counterpart of the ASCII form used by the Network Virtual Terminal. UTF-8 was chosen because it is compatible with ASCII and because of the IETF character set policy in RFC 2277.
sections.plainLanguage: Most Internet protocols were written when all text was plain ASCII letters and digits. Text in other languages had no agreed form, so this RFC picks one: UTF-8, the same way of encoding characters that the web already uses, together with fixed rules for line endings and for how the text is written before it is sent.

sections.title: The Net-Unicode Rules
sections.content:
Section 2 defines the format in six rules. Characters must be encoded in UTF-8. Where the protocol has the concept of lines, a line ending must be a carriage return (CR, U+000D) followed by a line feed (LF, U+000A), and CR should not appear anywhere else except immediately before LF or in the sequence CR NUL, which is not recommended.

The control characters in the ASCII range, U+0000 to U+001F and U+007F to U+009F, should generally be avoided. Space, CR, LF and form feed are the exceptions, and the form feed is to be used with caution, since it has no standard meaning and a page length assumed by the sender may not suit the receiver. The C1 controls, U+0080 through U+009F, which did not exist in ASCII, must not appear at all.

Before transmission, all character sequences should be normalized in the Unicode normalization form NFC. The byte order mark signature must not appear at the start of these strings. And a system must not transmit any string containing a code point that is unassigned in the Unicode version it depends on; the version of NFC and the version of Unicode it uses must match.

The RFC is explicit about line endings. Lines end in CRLF and only in CRLF; anything that does not end in CRLF is either not a line or is severely malformed. The newer characters IND (U+0084) and NEL (U+0085) must not be used to mark lines, nor the line and paragraph separators at U+2028 and U+2029, because their use has not been established on the Internet, many protocols require CRLF, and they fall inside the C1 controls group.
sections.plainLanguage: The format is short: encode the characters as UTF-8, end every line with a carriage return and a line feed, keep control characters out of the text, put the text into normal form before sending it, and leave out any character that the sender's version of Unicode has not yet given a meaning to.

sections.title: Normalizing the Text
sections.content:
Some strings of Unicode are fundamentally equivalent: they represent the same text. The Unicode Standard calls these canonical equivalents. The RFC gives two examples. The ohm sign at U+2126 and the Greek capital letter omega at U+03A9 are the same character written two ways. The Latin small letter a at U+0061 followed by the combining grave accent at U+0300 is the same character as the Latin small letter a with grave at U+00E0.

Comparing strings becomes much easier when such cases always appear in one single form. The Unicode Consortium specifies a normalization form, NFC, that maps every canonically equivalent sequence onto one unique form. In practice it produces a precomposed character whenever one exists, and it reorders combining marks so that their order is unique and unambiguous.

Of the normalization forms Unicode defines, the RFC picks NFC because it is closest to everyday use, because it minimizes the side effects of treating characters as equivalent when they may not be equivalent in every situation, and because it usually takes the least work to convert from a non-Unicode encoding.

Since some applications rely on operating system or library functions they do not control, and since the robustness principle says a receiver should cope, the RFC says that receivers of Net-Unicode strings should be ready to receive strings that were not normalized, and should not react to that in extreme ways.
sections.plainLanguage: The same letter can be written in more than one way, for example as one combined character or as a letter followed by a mark. The RFC asks senders to use the combined form, so that two texts that look the same also match when a program compares them.

sections.title: Unicode Versions and Stability
sections.content:
Unicode grows over time. New versions arrive at regular intervals and add scripts and characters, and occasionally change a property definition. In retrospect, one advantage of ASCII was that its code space was full when the Standard was published, so characters could hardly be added or changed.

The RFC argues that new Unicode versions should not disturb a Net-Unicode stream. The transformation between a code point and its UTF-8 bytes is algorithmic and does not depend on whether the code point has been assigned, and the recommended normalization form, NFC, performs a very limited set of mappings, far fewer than the more extensive NFKC used in Nameprep.

The NFC tables may be updated as characters are added, but the Unicode Consortium has guaranteed the stability of all NFC strings: if a string contains no unassigned characters and is normalized in NFC, it will still be normalized in NFC in every future version of the Standard. The stability of the format therefore depends on implementations not allowing unassigned characters.

Code points reserved for private use have no standard definitions and no normalization interpretations, so they should be avoided in strings meant for Internet interchange. The specification applies to Unicode versions starting at version 5.0 and continuing up to, but not including, any version that changes the UTF-8 definition or the stability of NFC. The RFC also says that a protocol which refers to it should treat a received string that looks like UTF-8 and is not otherwise identified, for example by a character set label, as UTF-8.
sections.plainLanguage: Unicode keeps growing, so a format built on it has to survive new characters being added. The RFC relies on a promise from the Unicode Consortium that already-normalized text stays normalized, and on a rule that senders leave out characters that Unicode has not defined yet.

sections.title: Where the Format Applies
sections.content:
The RFC explains where Net-Unicode fits. The individual media types used in email and with HTTP have their own rules about UTF-8 and normalization, and the application transports impose their own line ending conventions, so this specification is not meant to change them. It is meant for specifications that have not yet defined how to use Unicode, and for protocols that depend on the original Telnet design, or on other arrangements that need a standard, interoperable definition of a string without a content label. Whois, specified in RFC 3912, is given as an example of a member of that group.

The RFC then faces the practical problem of Unicode versions. Each new version brings new characters and sometimes new combining characters, and version 5.0 introduced sequences of characters named as if they were single characters. NFC is stable only if strings are transmitted and stored normalized, if corrections are never made to character definitions or normalization tables, and if unassigned code points are never used, because an unassigned code point always normalizes to itself and might later be assigned to a character that takes part in some other mapping.

The RFC lists four ways to handle this. Freeze on one version of Unicode and forbid the use of unassigned characters. Require every text string to start with a version indication, which the RFC calls impractical. Design a different set of normalization rules that never maps an unassigned code point to anything but itself. Or devise a process like NFC that rejects code points that are unassigned in the current version instead of mapping them to themselves, which the Unicode Consortium has discussed under the name Stable NFC. The RFC picks the last as a reasonable compromise, because no approach can be as stable and predictable as ASCII while Unicode keeps growing.
sections.plainLanguage: The format is for protocols that have not yet settled how to handle text in other languages. Because Unicode keeps adding characters, the RFC also had to decide how the format survives that, and it settles on a compromise: keep the normal form rules but refuse characters that the sender's Unicode version has not defined.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most of the security issues that apply to UTF-8 in RFC 3629 apply here too, though the requirement to normalize and the extra restrictions make this format slightly less exposed to some of them. A shift in Unicode versions can introduce other issues.

Programs that receive these streams should be very careful about assuming that the incoming data is normalized, since unnormalized forms, and invalid UTF-8, could be used as part of an attack. Firewalls and other systems that interpret UTF-8 should be built with the clear knowledge that an attacker may deliberately send unnormalized text, for instance to get past a naive text-matching system that looks for a particular string of characters.

The RFC repeats the NVT rule that CR must be followed by LF or NUL. NUL, the octet with all bits zero, is a trap for programming languages that use it as a string terminator, and that is an extra reason to avoid CR altogether apart from the sequence CR LF.

Finally, the discussion of Unicode versions rests on several assumptions: that future versions behave as described, that NFC is applied properly, and that UTF-8 is processed and transmitted exactly as specified in RFC 3629. If any of those assumptions fail, strings that should be considered equivalent may not compare equal, and robust code has to be ready for that.
sections.plainLanguage: The main warning is that a receiver cannot trust the text to be in normal form, because an attacker could send text that looks the same to a person but is written differently, to slip past a system that searches for exact strings. Receivers should therefore compare text in a way that treats equivalent spellings as equal, and should keep their text handling robust.

sections.title: How the Internet Got Its Text Format
sections.content:
The appendices give the background. One of the earliest ARPANET design decisions was to standardize on a single coding for text so that every host could translate to and from it. The participating host systems used at least three character codings: BCD, EBCDIC, which was tied to one hardware vendor, and the then-new ASCII. Because the project was open and EBCDIC belonged to one vendor, the Network Working Group chose ASCII, in the form of seven-bit ASCII in an eight-bit field, as a compromise between hosts that used seven-bit characters, eight-bit characters, or nine-bit fields.

Work on the Telnet protocol led to the Network Virtual Terminal, whose character conventions included carriage return followed by line feed as the common way to end a line, because the host systems disagreed about line endings. Since NVT ASCII was restricted to seven-bit characters, the high-order bit was reserved for control signalling. The idea was that a system could use whatever coding was convenient locally, but text sent over the network had to follow the one convention. Telnet, the command stream and ASCII type in FTP, the message stream in SMTP, and the strings passed to finger and whois all assumed this model. HTTP followed the same general model but allowed eight-bit data and left the line ending sequence unspecified, which the RFC notes has caused a significant number of problems.

The RFC also reviews the ASCII NVT definition and updates it. The control codes that were defined but not required, BEL, BS, HT, VT and FF, should not be used except in exceptional circumstances, because their original printer definitions are no longer in general use and their effects differ between systems. CR should generally appear only before LF, LF CR should not appear except as a side effect of several CRLF sequences in a row, and bare LF and HT are problematic because their effects are not uniform.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet settled on ASCII early on so that every computer could read the same text, and then built the Telnet idea of a standard imaginary terminal on top of it. Most later protocols assumed that convention. This RFC keeps the line ending rule and the useful parts of the old rules, but drops the control characters whose meaning was never the same on every machine.

viz.caption: The six rules that define Net-Unicode

items.title: UTF-8
items.text: Characters must be encoded in UTF-8.

items.title: CRLF
items.text: A line ends with a carriage return followed by a line feed.

items.title: Few control characters
items.text: Control characters should be avoided, and the C1 controls must not appear.

items.title: NFC
items.text: Text should be normalized in Unicode form NFC before transmission.

items.title: No byte order mark
items.text: The byte order mark signature must not start the string.

items.title: No unassigned characters
items.text: Code points that the sender's Unicode version has not assigned must not be sent.
